newsitem.title: USA: Ford first-quarter profits more than double.
newsitem.headline: Ford first-quarter profits more than double.

text.p: Ford Motor Co., reaping the rewards of a cost-cutting crusade, Wednesday posted first-quarter earnings of $1.47 billion, more than double last year's $653 million.
On a per-share basis, Ford reported earnings of $1.20, beating the Wall Street consensus estimate of about 90 cents a share. A year ago, Ford had per share earnings of 53 cents.
Profits from Ford's U.S. automotive operations, which contribute about two-thirds of its total automotive revenue, soared to $836 million from $48 million a year ago.

Ford's first-quarter profits from worldwide automotive operations were also up sharply, to $1 billion from $142 million a year ago, thanks to smaller losses in South America and a profit rebound in Europe.
Total revenues rose to $36.2 billion from $35.2 billion.

Ford, the last of the Big Three to report first quarter results, brings the U.S. automakers' combined net profits to $4.29 billion. That compares with $2.46 billion a year ago, when General Motors Corp. was hampered by a strike and Ford was enduring heavy launch costs.

Earlier this week, GM reported first quarter earnings of $1.79 billion, vs. $800 million a year ago. Chrysler Corp. last week posted first quarter earnings of $1.03 billion, a 2.4 percent rise from $1.0 billion.
Ford stock rose $1.50 to $34.75 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was among the most actively traded shares.
"The changes we have been making to our automotive operations for the past two years are beginning to pay off," Ford Chairman Alex Trotman said in a statement.

In the first quarter, Ford slashed its total automotive costs by $800 million, amounting to what Chief Financial Officer John Devine called a "fast start" to the company's goal of cutting automotive costs by $1 billion in 1997.

Devine, speaking at a news briefing, said the savings came from cuts across the board and preplanned cost-cutting measures that were moved up to showcase the company's war on costs and efforts to improve its core automotive results. But he cautioned that rate will probably not be matched for the rest of the year.
"I don't want you to multiply 800 times four," he said.
Indeed, Devine and analysts stressed the company is facing increasingly tough competition, particularly in the United States and Europe.

Although total U.S. sales this year are expected to be about even with the 15.4 million units of 1996, high volume products from Japanese automakers are forcing Ford to keep incentives high, further squeezing already thin car profit margins, analysts said.
"It's essentially a race between the company's falling costs and the market's deteriorating profitability," said John Casesa, an analyst with Schroder Wertheim.
Ford has taken several high-profile steps to reduce its costs, including discontinuing five vehicle models in the United States and cutting back its factories in Europe and Brazil.
Ford's first quarter also benefited from sales of high-profit margin products such as the F-Series pickup trucks and Expedition full-size sport utility vehicle.

A year ago, Ford's results were hampered by a number of high-volume product launches, both in the United States and Europe, such as the new Ford Fiesta small car and the redesigned F-Series pickups. Worldwide vehicle unit sales for the first quarter were up to 1,681,000 from 1,638,000.
As Ford's automotive results improve, the red-hot earnings streak of its Financial Services Group is slowing down.
For the first time in several quarters, Financial Services' first-quarter net income was below that of the automotive unit.

Financial Services earned $465 million in the quarter, down from a record $511 million. Pulling down the total were lower earnings from Ford Credit, which fell to $276 million from $339 million, and the sale of most USL Capital assets last year.
Devine said the higher credit losses that Ford Credit suffered in the first quarter are likely to continue through the year and be a drag on earnings.
